notes.b: Volumetric analysis uses a measured volume of reaction to find an unknown concentration. It is the basis of every titration, so the terms here are used throughout the subsection.
points: Volumetric analysis (titration) finds the concentration of a solution, the analyte (the solution being analysed), by measuring the volume that reacts exactly with a known volume of another solution of known concentration.
The calculation depends on knowing one concentration exactly, so at least one of the two solutions must be a standard solution (a solution whose concentration is accurately known).
Titre: the volume of solution added from the burette (the long graduated glass tube with a tap, used to add measured volumes of liquid).
End point: the point at which the indicator (a substance that changes colour depending on whether the solution is acidic or basic) changes colour.
Equivalence point: the point at which the reactants have reacted in exactly the mole ratio of the balanced equation (the ratio of the numbers of moles shown by the coefficients).
A good indicator is one whose end point coincides with the equivalence point, so that the colour change tells you the moment the reaction is exactly complete.
notes.tip: Learn the three terms separately: the titre is a volume, the end point is the colour change you see, and the equivalence point is when the reactants have reacted in exactly the ratio of the balanced equation.

notes.b: A titration answer can only be as good as the solution it is measured against. That is why one special type of substance, the primary standard, is used to fix the concentration.
points: A primary standard is a very pure, stable substance of known formula that can be weighed accurately and dissolved to give a standard solution directly. There is more on this in Solutions and concentration.
Acid–base primary standard: anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ (anhydrous means it contains no water of crystallisation, so its formula and mass are exact).
Redox primary standard: ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O. Redox titrations are ones where electrons are transferred, and this is mentioned here only as an example.
Every result in volumetric analysis is only as accurate as the standard: an impure or unstable standard gives a wrong concentration, and so a wrong answer for the analyte.
notes.tip: If asked for the importance of a primary standard, say that the calculation depends on one concentration being exactly known, give its properties (very pure, stable, known formula, weighed accurately), and name Na₂CO₃ as the acid–base example.

notes.b: Some reagents cannot be made up directly as standard solutions, because their concentration changes or cannot be known from the mass weighed out. Their concentration must instead be found by titration, a process called standardisation.
points: Sodium hydroxide absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, so the mass weighed out is not all NaOH.
Hydrochloric acid is volatile (it evaporates easily, so hydrogen chloride is lost from the solution).
Potassium manganate(VII) solution slowly decomposes, especially in light and in the presence of organic matter, forming MnO₂.
Sodium thiosulfate crystals have an uncertain water content, so their formula mass, and the number of moles weighed out, is uncertain.
Standardisation is finding the exact concentration of such a solution by titrating it against a primary standard, or against a solution already standardised against one.
Example: hydrochloric acid is standardised by titration against a standard solution of sodium carbonate: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
Example: sodium hydroxide is then standardised against the standardised hydrochloric acid, and potassium manganate(VII) is standardised against ammonium iron(II) sulfate.
A solution standardised in this way is sometimes called a secondary standard.
notes.tip: Exams ask why sodium hydroxide is not a primary standard: it absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air. You may also be asked to explain standardisation and how hydrochloric acid is standardised, so learn the Na₂CO₃ equation.

notes.b: A titration uses a small set of apparatus, each with a specific job. Knowing what each item is for lets you explain why it is used.
points: Pipette, used with a pipette filler (a rubber bulb that draws liquid up): delivers an exact volume, e.g. 25.0 cm³, of one solution into a conical flask.
Burette: delivers measured, variable volumes of the other solution, read to 0.05 cm³.
Conical flask: can be swirled without splashing, and holds the pipetted solution during the titration.
White tile: placed under the flask so that the colour change shows clearly.
Funnel: used to fill the burette and then removed.
Wash bottle of deionised water (water with dissolved ions removed): used to rinse the apparatus and to wash down the flask.
Indicator: added to the conical flask.
Diagram: a burette clamped above a conical flask on a white tile, with the pipette and pipette filler shown separately; label burette, tap, pipette, pipette filler, conical flask and white tile.
notes.tip: Exams ask why a white tile is used (so the colour change shows clearly) and why the flask is swirled. Label every item in your diagram.

notes.b: Each rinse removes water or other solution that would dilute the solution it is about to hold. Following the steps in order, with the reason for each, is what the exam asks for.
points: Rinse the pipette with deionised water, then with a little of the solution it is to measure, so that any water left in it does not dilute the solution.
Draw the solution up above the mark using a pipette filler, then let it down until the bottom of the meniscus (the curved surface of the liquid) sits on the mark at eye level.

Let the solution run into the conical flask, touching the tip against the inside of the flask at the end; do not blow out the last drop, because the pipette is calibrated (marked to deliver an exact volume) to allow for it.
Rinse the burette with deionised water, then with the solution it is to contain, so that any water left in it does not dilute the solution.
Fill the burette using a funnel, then remove the funnel, because drips from it would change the reading.
Run a little solution out through the tap to fill the part below the tap and remove any air bubble, which would otherwise make the volume delivered inaccurate.
Read the burette at eye level, from the bottom of the meniscus.
Rinsing the conical flask with deionised water is fine, because it does not change the number of moles in the pipetted volume.
The conical flask must not be rinsed with either solution, because that would leave extra moles of reagent in the flask.
notes.tip: The pipette and burette are rinsed with their own solutions; the conical flask is not. Exams ask for the correct procedure for rinsing and filling them and why each rinse is needed.

notes.b: A titration is done twice over: a quick rough run to find roughly where the end point is, then careful accurate runs. Each step is there to make the final volume as precise as possible.
points: Add two or three drops of the indicator to the conical flask.
Add solution from the burette while swirling the flask; first do a rough titration to find the approximate end point.
In the accurate titrations, add the solution quickly to within about 1 cm³ of the rough titre, then add it drop by drop, swirling, until one drop gives a permanent colour change.
Wash the inside walls of the flask with deionised water near the end point, so that all the reagent reacts.
Repeat until two accurate titres agree to within 0.1 cm³, then average them, leaving out the rough titre.
notes.tip: Do not include the rough titre in the mean. Exams ask how the end point is detected, why you wash down the sides and why you swirl.

notes.h: Strong acid–strong base: hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide
notes.b: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid and sodium hydroxide a strong base, meaning each ionises fully in water. This is the simplest titration, with a 1 : 1 mole ratio.
points: Equation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l), with a mole ratio of 1 : 1.
Indicator: phenolphthalein, which changes from colourless to pink as NaOH is added from the burette, or methyl orange.
Either indicator works because the pH (the scale of acidity) changes sharply over a wide range at the equivalence point.
Sample data: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH needs a mean titre of 22.5 cm³ of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ HCl.
Moles NaOH = 2.25 × 10⁻³ mol, because the mole ratio is 1 : 1.
Concentration of NaOH = 2.25 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.0900 mol L⁻¹.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name a suitable indicator and give its colour change, and to calculate the concentration from titration data. Take the mole ratio from the balanced equation.

notes.h: Strong acid–weak base: hydrochloric acid and sodium carbonate
notes.b: Sodium carbonate is the primary standard used to standardise hydrochloric acid. It is a weak base (one that ionises only partly in water), and the mole ratio is not 1 : 1, so the equation must be used in the calculation.
points: Equation: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), with a mole ratio of Na₂CO₃ : HCl of 1 : 2.
Indicator: methyl orange, which is yellow in the sodium carbonate and turns orange-red at the end point as acid is added.
Phenolphthalein is unsuitable because it changes colour in alkaline solution, before the end point.
Sample data: 25.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol L⁻¹ Na₂CO₃ needs 23.8 cm³ of HCl.
Moles HCl = 2 × 1.25 × 10⁻³ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol, because the mole ratio is 1 : 2.
Concentration of HCl = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.0238 L = 0.105 mol L⁻¹.
Ammonia, a weak base, is titrated with hydrochloric acid in the same way, using methyl orange: NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq).
notes.tip: The mole ratio must come from the balanced equation: 1 : 2 for Na₂CO₃ : HCl. Name methyl orange with its colour change, and say that phenolphthalein is unsuitable because it changes colour in alkaline solution, before the end point.

notes.b: The solutions used in these titrations can harm skin and eyes, so a few precautions apply every time.
points: Wear goggles: sodium hydroxide is corrosive (it burns tissue), especially to the eyes, and hydrochloric acid is corrosive or irritant.
Use a pipette filler, never the mouth, so that no solution is swallowed.
Fill the burette while it is below eye level, for example by lowering it or removing it from the stand, so that you do not spill solution towards your face.

keyTerms.definition: A method that finds the concentration of one solution from the measured volume that reacts exactly with a known volume of another solution.
The solution whose concentration is being found in a titration.
A solution whose concentration is known exactly.
A very pure, stable substance of known formula that can be weighed accurately to make a standard solution directly.
Finding the exact concentration of a solution by titrating it against a primary standard or a solution already standardised against one.
A solution whose concentration has been fixed by standardisation against a primary standard.
The volume of solution added from the burette in a titration.
The point at which the indicator changes colour during a titration.
The point at which the reactants have reacted in exactly the mole ratio of the balanced equation.
Apparatus that delivers one fixed, exact volume of a solution, such as 25.0 cm³.
A graduated tube with a tap that delivers measured, variable volumes of solution, read to 0.05 cm³.
The curved upper surface of a liquid, read at its bottom edge in a burette or pipette.
A quick first titration done to find the approximate end point, whose titre is left out of the mean.
The ratio of the amounts, in moles, of reactants and products given by the coefficients in a balanced equation.
An indicator that is colourless in acid and pink in alkaline solution, changing colour over about pH 8.3–10.
An indicator that is red in acid and yellow in alkaline solution, changing colour over about pH 3.1–4.4.

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of a primary standard in volumetric analysis and name one primary standard used in acid–base titrations.
questions.model: Volumetric analysis finds the concentration of an analyte from the volume that reacts with a known volume of another solution, so at least one of the two solutions must be a standard solution whose concentration is known exactly. A primary standard is a very pure, stable substance of known formula that can be weighed accurately and dissolved to give a standard solution directly. Its importance is that every result is only as accurate as the standard: an impure or unstable standard gives a wrong concentration and therefore a wrong answer for the analyte. One primary standard used in acid–base titrations is anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃.

questions.prompt: What is meant by standardising a solution? Explain why hydrochloric acid must be standardised before it is used in a titration.
questions.model: Standardising a solution is finding its exact concentration by titrating it against a primary standard, or against a solution already standardised against one. Hydrochloric acid must be standardised because it is volatile, so it cannot be made up directly as a standard solution and its concentration is not known exactly. It is therefore titrated against a standard solution of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g), and the exact concentration found is then used in later titrations.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would rinse and fill a burette and a pipette, and how you would carry out a titration accurately, explaining the reason for each rinse.
questions.model: Rinse the pipette with deionised water, then with a little of the solution it is to measure, so that water left in it does not dilute the solution. Using a pipette filler, draw the solution up above the mark, then let it down until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the mark at eye level. Let the solution run into the conical flask, touching the tip against the inside of the flask, and do not blow out the last drop because the pipette is calibrated to allow for it. Rinse the burette with deionised water, then with the solution it is to contain, so that water left in it does not dilute the solution. Fill it using a funnel, then remove the funnel, because drips from it would change the reading. Run a little solution out through the tap to fill the part below the tap and remove any air bubble, then read the burette at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus. Rinse the conical flask with deionised water only, because this does not change the number of moles in the pipetted volume; it must not be rinsed with either solution. Add two or three drops of indicator to the flask. Add solution from the burette while swirling, doing a rough titration first to find the approximate end point. In the accurate titrations, add the solution quickly to within about 1 cm³ of the rough titre, then drop by drop, swirling, until one drop gives a permanent colour change. Wash the inside walls of the flask with deionised water near the end point so that all the reagent reacts. Repeat until two accurate titres agree to within 0.1 cm³, then average them, leaving out the rough titre.

questions.prompt: 25.0 cm³ of a sodium carbonate solution required 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid for neutralisation using methyl orange. Write the balanced equation and calculate the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution in mol L⁻¹.
questions.model: Balanced equation: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Moles HCl = 0.150 × 0.0200 = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol. The mole ratio of Na₂CO₃ : HCl is 1 : 2, so moles Na₂CO₃ = 3.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 2 = 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol. Concentration of Na₂CO₃ = 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.0600 mol L⁻¹.
